questions.stem: Briefly explain why and how a galvanometer is converted into an ammeter.
questions.solution:
An ammeter is a current measuring device, so its resistance should be zero in the ideal case. Thus, in order to minimize its resistance according to the required range, we connect a suitable resistance in parallel with it, which is called shunt $S$, as shown.
$$R_S = \frac{I_g}{I - I_g}R_g$$

questions.stem: How are infrared waves produced ? Why are these waves referred to as heat waves ? Give any two uses of infrared waves.
questions.solution:
Infrared waves are produced by hot bodies and molecules. These waves produce heating effect, so they are also known as heat waves or thermal radiation.
Uses of infrared waves :
(i) In the remote control of a TV or VCR, the keypad of which contains a small infrared transmitter.
(ii) Infrared lamps in the treatment of muscular complaints.
questions.or_stem: How are X-rays produced ? Give any two uses of these.
questions.or_solution:
X-rays are produced by sudden deceleration of fast moving electrons by a metal target.
Uses of X-rays:
(i) In medical diagnosis because X-rays can pass through flesh but not through bones.
(ii) In the study of crystal structure because X-rays can be reflected and diffracted by crystals.

questions.stem: In the given figure the radius of curvature of curved face in the plano-convex and the plano-concave lens is $15\ \mathrm{cm}$ each. The refractive index of the material of the lenses is $1.5$. Find the final position of the image formed.
questions.solution:
Let $L_1$ be the plano-convex lens and $L_2$ the plano-concave lens.
$$\frac{1}{f_1} = (1.5 - 1)\left[\frac{1}{\infty} + \frac{1}{15}\right] \Rightarrow \frac{1}{f_1} = \frac{0.5}{15} \Rightarrow f_1 = 30\ \mathrm{cm}$$
$$\frac{1}{f_2} = (1.5 - 1)\left[-\frac{1}{15} + 0\right] \Rightarrow f_2 = -30\ \mathrm{cm}$$
Using lens formula for $L_1$:
$$\frac{1}{f_1} = \frac{1}{v_1} - \frac{1}{u_1}$$
$$\frac{1}{30} = \frac{1}{v_1} + \frac{1}{\infty}$$
$$v_1 = 30\ \mathrm{cm}$$
Using lens formula for $L_2$:
$$\frac{1}{f_2} = \frac{1}{v_2} - \frac{1}{u_2}$$
$$-\frac{1}{30} = \frac{1}{v_2} - \frac{1}{10} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v_2} = \frac{1}{10} - \frac{1}{30}$$
$$\Rightarrow \frac{3 - 1}{30} = \frac{2}{30} \Rightarrow v_2 = 15\ \mathrm{cm}$$
Final image is formed at $35\ \mathrm{cm}$ towards right from plano-convex lens.

questions.stem:
What happens to the interference pattern when two coherent sources are
(a) Infinitely close, and
(b) far apart from each other.
questions.solution:
(a) Linear fringe width $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$
If we decrease $d$ ($\downarrow$) then $\beta$ increases ($\uparrow$). So no interference pattern is detected.
(b) Fringe width $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} \Rightarrow \beta \propto \dfrac{1}{d}$
If we increase $d$ ($\uparrow$) then fringe width ($\beta$) will be small, so that the fringes are not resolved and they do not appear separate. That's why interference pattern is not detected.

questions.solution:
The amount of energy required to remove an electron from an isolated atom or molecule.
Ionization energy for hydrogen $= 13.6\ \mathrm{eV}$
questions.or_stem: Define the term, mass defect. How is it related to stability of the nucleus?
questions.or_solution: The difference between total mass of nucleus (protons and neutrons) and actual mass of nucleus is mass defect. If mass defect is large, the binding energy is also large, so binding energy per nucleon is also large and stability increases.

questions.stem: Two charged conducting spheres of radii $a$ and $b$ are connected to each other by a wire. Find the ratio of the electric fields at their surfaces.
questions.solution:
Let $a$ be the radius of sphere A, $Q_A$ the charge on sphere A and $C_A$ the capacitance of sphere A.
Let $b$ be the radius of sphere B, $Q_B$ the charge on sphere B and $C_B$ the capacitance of sphere B.
Since the two spheres are connected with a wire, their potential ($V$) will become equal.
$$E_A = \frac{kQ_A}{a^2},\quad E_B = \frac{kQ_B}{b^2}$$
$$\frac{E_A}{E_B} = \frac{Q_A}{Q_B} \times \frac{b^2}{a^2} \quad \ldots(1)$$
$Q = CV$, so $Q_A = C_A V$ and $Q_B = C_B V$
$$\frac{Q_A}{Q_B} = \frac{C_A}{C_B} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{C_A}{C_B} = \frac{a}{b} \qquad \{\text{from } C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 r\}$$
So, $$\frac{Q_A}{Q_B} = \frac{a}{b} \quad \ldots(2)$$
From eq. (1) and (2):
$$\frac{E_A}{E_B} = \frac{b}{a}$$
[The ratio of electric fields at the surface is $b/a$]
questions.or_stem:
A parallel plate capacitor (A) of capacitance $C$ is charged by a battery to voltage $V$. The battery is disconnected and an uncharged capacitor (B) of capacitance $2C$ is connected across A. Find the ratio of
(i) Final charges on A and B.
(ii) Total electrostatic energy stored in A and B finally and that stored in A initially.
questions.or_solution:
(i) $V_A = V_B$
$$\frac{q_A}{C_1} = \frac{q_B}{C_2}$$
$$\frac{q_A}{C} = \frac{q_B}{2C} \Rightarrow q_A = \frac{q_B}{2}$$
$q_A + q_B = CV$
$q_A + 2q_A = CV$
Final charge on A: $q_A = \dfrac{CV}{3}$
Charge on B: $q_B = \dfrac{2}{3}CV$
$$\frac{q_A}{q_B} = \frac{CV/3}{2CV/3} = \frac{1}{2}$$
(ii) Final potential $V = \dfrac{q}{C}$
$$V_A = \frac{CV}{3 \times C} = \frac{V}{3}$$
also similarly $V_B = \dfrac{V}{3}$
Energy stored in A: $U = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^{2}$
Total electrostatic energy stored in capacitors A and B:
$$U_f = \frac{1}{2}C_{eq.} \times \left(\frac{V}{3}\right)^{2} = \frac{1}{2} \times 3C \times \frac{V^{2}}{9} = \frac{1}{6}CV^{2}$$
Then,
$$\frac{U_f}{U_A} = \frac{CV^{2}/6}{CV^{2}/2} = \frac{1}{3}$$

questions.stem: Define current density and relaxation time. Derive an expression for resistivity of a conductor in terms of number density of charge carriers in the conductor and relaxation time.
questions.solution:
Current density : It is defined as the current passing per unit cross sectional area of a conductor, normally.
Relaxation time : The average time between two successive collisions of electrons, when electric field is applied.
We know that the current flowing through the conductor is :
$$I = nAev_d$$
$$\therefore I = neA\left(\frac{eE\tau}{m}\right)$$
Using $E = \dfrac{V}{\ell}$
$$I = neA\left(\frac{eV}{m\ell}\right)\tau = \left(\frac{ne^{2}A\tau}{m\ell}\right)V = \frac{1}{R}V$$
$I \propto V \rightarrow$ which is Ohm's law
Where $R = \dfrac{m\ell}{nAe^{2}\tau}$ is constant for a particular conductor at a particular temperature and is called the resistance of the conductor.
$$R = \left(\frac{m}{ne^{2}\tau}\right)\frac{\ell}{A} = \frac{\rho\ell}{A} \Rightarrow \rho = \left(\frac{m}{ne^{2}\tau}\right)$$
Where $\rho$ is the specific resistance or resistivity of the material of the wire. It depends on number of free electrons per unit volume and temperature.

questions.stem: A series CR circuit with $R = 200\ \Omega$ and $C = (50/\pi)\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ is connected across an ac source of peak voltage $\varepsilon_0 = 100\ \mathrm{V}$ and frequency $\nu = 50\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Calculate (a) impedance of the circuit ($Z$). (b) phase angle ($\phi$) and (c) voltage across the resistor.
questions.solution:
$R = 200\ \Omega$
$C = \dfrac{50}{\pi} \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{F}$
$\varepsilon_0 = 100\ \mathrm{V}$
$\nu = 50\ \mathrm{Hz}$
$$X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times \frac{50}{\pi} \times 10^{-6}} = 200\ \Omega$$
(a) $Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + X_C^{2}}$
$$= \sqrt{(200)^{2} + (200)^{2}} = 200\sqrt{2}\ \Omega$$
(b) $\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = \dfrac{200}{200\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
$\phi = 45^\circ$
(c) $V_R = IR$
$$= \frac{V}{Z} \times R = \frac{100}{\sqrt{2} \times 200\sqrt{2}} \times 200 \qquad \left\{V = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}} = V_{rms}\right\}$$
$V_R = 50\ \mathrm{V}$

questions.stem: Define critical angle for a given pair of media and total internal reflection. Obtain the relation between the critical angle and refractive index of the medium.
questions.solution:
Critical angle : It is the value of angle of incidence in denser medium, at which light ray refracts at $90^\circ$.
Total internal reflection (TIR) : When a ray of light enters from denser to rarer medium at an incident angle more than critical angle then the ray of light is totally reflected back in the same medium. This phenomenon is known as TIR.
We know that $\mu = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$
$i = i_c$, $r = 90^\circ$
$$_{d}\mu_{r} = \frac{\sin i_c}{\sin 90^\circ}$$
$$\frac{1}{_{r}\mu_{d}} = \sin i_c$$
$$\mu = {}_{r}\mu_{d} = \frac{1}{\sin i_c}$$

questions.stem:
(i) Distinguish between nuclear fission and fusion giving an example of each.
(ii) Explain the release of energy in nuclear fission and fusion on the basis of binding energy per nucleon curve.
questions.solution:
(i) Nuclear fission : Nuclear fission is the phenomenon of splitting of a heavy nucleus (usually $A > 230$) into two or more lighter nuclei.
Ex. $${}^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U} + {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} \rightarrow {}^{236}_{92}\mathrm{U} \rightarrow {}^{141}_{56}\mathrm{Ba} + {}^{92}_{36}\mathrm{Kr} + 3\,{}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} + Q$$
Nuclear fusion : The process of combining of two lighter nuclei to form one heavy nucleus is called nuclear fusion.
Ex. $$4\,{}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} + 2\,{}^{0}_{1}e + 2\nu + 26.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$$
(ii) Fission : B.E. of lighter nuclei formed is greater than that of the heavy parent nucleus, so excess energy is liberated in the form of heat.
Fusion : B.E. of the nucleus formed is much more than that of the nuclei forming it, so the difference of energy is liberated in the form of heat.
questions.or_stem:
(i) How is the size of a nucleus found experimentally? Write the relation between the radius and mass number of a nucleus.
(ii) Prove that the density of a nucleus is independent of its mass number.
questions.or_solution:
(i) Distance of closest approach ($r_0$) : Estimation of nuclear size
At the distance $r_0$ the entire kinetic energy of the $\alpha$-particle is converted into potential energy of the system.
$$\therefore\ \text{K.E.}(K) = \text{P.E.} = \frac{kq_1q_2}{r_0} = \frac{(K)(2e)\cdot Ze}{r_0}$$
$$\Rightarrow r_0 = \frac{Ze^{2}}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 K}$$
Size of a nucleus is experimentally estimated from Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment.
Radius $R$ of a nucleus of mass number $A$ is given by the relation
$R = R_0 [A]^{1/3}$
where $R_0 \rightarrow$ constant $= 1.2\ \mathrm{fm}$
(ii) If $m$ is the average mass of a nucleon, then mass of nucleus $= mA$ where $A$ is mass number.
$$\text{Density} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} = \frac{mA}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}} = \frac{mA}{\frac{4}{3}\pi\left(R_0 A^{1/3}\right)^{3}}$$
$$\rho = \frac{3m}{4\pi R_0^{3}}$$
So, density of nucleus is independent of mass number.

questions.stem:
(a) (i) Use Gauss law to obtain an expression for the electric field due to an infinitely long thin straight wire with uniform linear charge density $\lambda$.
(ii) An infinitely long positively charged straight wire has a linear charge density $\lambda$. An electron is revolving in a circle with a constant speed $v$ such that the wire passes through the centre, and is perpendicular to the plane, of the circle. Find the kinetic energy of the electron in terms of magnitudes of its charge and linear charge density $\lambda$ on the wire.
(iii) Draw a graph of kinetic energy as a function of linear charge density $\lambda$.
questions.solution:
(a) (i) To calculate the electric field, imagine a cylindrical Gaussian surface, since the field is everywhere radial, flux through two ends of the cylindrical Gaussian surface is zero.
At cylindrical part of the surface electric field $\vec{E}$ is normal to the surface at every point and its magnitude is constant.
Therefore flux through the Gaussian surface = flux through the curved cylindrical part of the surface.
$\phi = E \times 2\pi r\ell$ ......(i)
Applying Gauss's Law for cylindrical Gaussian surface
$\text{Flux } \phi = \frac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\epsilon_{0}}$
Total charge enclosed = Linear charge density $\times\ \ell$
$q_{\text{enclosed}} = \lambda \ell$
$\therefore\ \phi = \frac{\lambda \ell}{\epsilon_{0}}$ .......(ii)
Using Equations (i) & (ii)
$E \times 2\pi r\ell = \frac{\lambda \ell}{\epsilon_{0}} \Rightarrow E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_{0} r}$
$\vec{E} = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_{0} r}\hat{n}$
(where $\hat{n}$ is a unit vector normal to the line charge)
(ii) $F_c = F_e$
$\frac{mv^{2}}{r} = \frac{e\,2k\lambda}{r}$
$mv^{2} = e\,2k\lambda$
Kinetic energy (KE) $= \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = ek\lambda$
$\mathrm{KE} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 9 \times 10^{9} \times \lambda$
$\mathrm{KE} = 14.4 \times 10^{-10}\,\lambda\ \mathrm{J}$
(iii) (graph shown in the figure)

questions.stem:
(a) (i) Define coefficient of self-induction. Obtain an expression for self-inductance of a long solenoid of length $l$, area of cross-section $A$ having $N$ turns.
(ii) Calculate the self-inductance of a coil using the following data obtained when an AC source of frequency $\left(\frac{200}{\pi}\right)\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and a DC source is applied across the coil.

AC Source
S. No. | V (Volts) | I (A)
1 | 3.0 | 0.5
2 | 6.0 | 1.0
3 | 9.0 | 1.5

DC Source
S. No. | V (Volts) | I (A)
1 | 4.0 | 1.0
2 | 6.0 | 1.5
3 | 8.0 | 2.0
questions.solution:
(a) (i) Self inductance of a long solenoid:
Co-efficient of self-induction of a coil is defined as the e.m.f. induced in the coil per unit rate of change of current in the same coil
Magnetic field inside the solenoid due to current ($I$)
$B = \mu_0 n I$
$B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{l}$ $\left\{n = \frac{N}{l},\ N \Rightarrow \text{Total no. of turns}\right\}$
Flux linked with each turn
$\phi = BA \Rightarrow \left(\frac{\mu_0 N I}{l}\right)A$
Self inductance of solenoid
$L = \frac{N\phi}{I} \Rightarrow L = \frac{N}{I}\left(\frac{\mu_0 N I}{l}\right)A \Rightarrow L = \frac{\mu_0 N^{2} A}{l}$
(ii) Given frequency of AC source $(f) = \left(\frac{200}{\pi}\right)\mathrm{Hz}$
For AC source (in L-R circuit) $Z = \frac{3.0}{0.5} = 6\ \Omega$
For DC source (in R circuit) $R = \frac{4.0}{1.0} = 4\ \Omega$
$Z^{2} = R^{2} + X_L^{2} \Rightarrow 36 = 16 + X_L^{2}$
$X_L^{2} = 36 - 16 = 20$
$2\pi f L = 2\sqrt{5} \Rightarrow L = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\pi f} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\pi\left(\frac{200}{\pi}\right)} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{200} = 11.18\ \mathrm{mH}$
questions.or_stem:
(b) (i) With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the principle and working of an ac generator. Hence, obtain an expression for the instantaneous value of the emf generated.
(ii) The coil of an ac generator consists of 100 turns of wire, each of area $0.5\ \mathrm{m^{2}}$. The resistance of the wire is $100\ \Omega$. The coil is rotating in a magnetic field of $0.8\ \mathrm{T}$ perpendicular to its axis of rotation, at a constant angular speed of 60 radian per second. Calculate the maximum emf generated and power dissipated in the coil.
questions.or_solution:
(b) (i) Principle : It is based on electromagnetic induction.
When the armature coil rotates between magnetic poles with constant angular velocity ($\omega$) then the magnetic flux linked with the armature coil changes with time. The magnetic flux passing through coil is given by
$\phi = BA\cos\theta$, where $\theta \Rightarrow$ Angle between $\vec{B}$ and $\vec{A}$
$\phi = BA\cos\omega t$, $\theta = \omega t$
$B_1$ & $B_2$ are carbon brushes. $S_1$ & $S_2$ are slip rings.
Let at any instant ($t$), the angle between $\vec{B}$ and $\vec{A}$ is $\theta$, then the magnetic flux linked with coil at that instant.
$\phi_B = N\left(\vec{B}\cdot\vec{A}\right) = NBA\cos\theta$ ($N$ = Number of turns in the coil, $A$ = Area of the coil, $\omega$ = Angular velocity of coil)
$\phi_B = NBA\cos\omega t$ $\{\because \theta = \omega t\}$
$\frac{d\phi_B}{dt} = NBA\omega(-\sin\omega t)$
Thus induced emf, $e = -\frac{d\phi_B}{dt}$
or $e = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$
$e = e_0 \sin\omega t$ $\{\because e_0 = NBA\omega\}$
(ii) Given, $N = 100$, $A = 0.5\ \mathrm{m^{2}}$, $R = 100$ ohm, $B = 0.8\ \mathrm{T}$ & $\omega = 60$ radian per second
Maximum emf $\epsilon_0 = NBA\omega = 100 \times 0.5 \times 0.8 \times 60$
$\epsilon_0 = 2400$ volt
Power dissipated in the coil
$p = \frac{\epsilon_0^{2}}{R} = \frac{2400 \times 2400}{100} = 57600$ watt

questions.stem:
(a) (i) State Huygen's principle. With the help of a diagram, show how a plane wave is reflected from a surface. Hence verify the law of reflection.
(ii) A concave mirror of focal length $12\ \mathrm{cm}$ forms a three times magnified virtual image of an object. Find the distance of the object from the mirror.
questions.solution:
(a) (i) According to Huygens principle "each point on a wave front is a source of new disturbance, called secondary wavelets. These wavelets are spherical and travel with speed of light in that medium".
Let speed of the wave in the medium be '$v$'
Let the time taken by the wave front, to advance from point B to point C is '$\tau$'
Hence $BC = v\tau$
Let CE represent the reflected wave front, Distance $AE = v\tau = BC$
$\Delta AEC$ and $\Delta ABC$ are congruent
$\therefore\ \angle ABC = \angle AEC (90^\circ)$
$AC = AC$
$AE = BC$,
So, $\angle BAC = \angle ECA$ (by C.P.C.T.)
$\Rightarrow\ \angle i = \angle r$ (proved)
This is the law of reflections.
Incident & reflected rays lie in a same plane.
(ii) For concave mirror, focal length, $f = -12\ \mathrm{cm}$ Magnification, $m = +3$
$m = -\frac{v}{u} = 3 \Rightarrow v = -3u$
Applying mirror formula, $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{-12} = -\frac{1}{3u} + \frac{1}{u}$
$\frac{1}{-12} = \frac{-1+3}{3u} \Rightarrow u = -8\ \mathrm{cm}$
Hence, position of object is $-8\ \mathrm{cm}$.

(ii) The focal lengths of the objective and the eye-piece of a compound microscope are $1.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $2.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ respectively. Find the tube length of the microscope for obtaining a magnification of 300.
questions.or_solution:
(b) (i) Refracting telescope : (ray diagram shown in the figure)
Refracting type telescope consists of an objective lens of large aperture and large focal length whereas eyepiece is of small aperture and small focal length.
Magnifying Power : It is the ratio of visual angle subtended by final image at eye to the visual angle subtended by an object.
$M = \frac{\beta}{\alpha}$ {if $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are very small, $\alpha \approx \tan\alpha$ and $\beta \approx \tan\beta$}
Limitations of refracting telescope :
(1) Defect of chromatic aberration occurs in refracting type telescope.
(2) It has small resolving power.
(ii) Magnification of microscope
$M = \frac{L}{f_0} \times \frac{D}{f_e}$
$300 = \frac{L}{1.0} \times \frac{25}{2.0} \Rightarrow L = \frac{300}{25} \times 2.5 = 30\ \mathrm{cm}$ (length of tube)

questions.stem:
Consider the experimental set up shown in the figure. This jumping ring experiment is an outstanding demonstration of some simple laws of Physics. A conducting non-magnetic ring is placed over the vertical core of a solenoid. When current is passed through the solenoid, the ring is thrown off.

Answer the following questions :
(i) Explain the reason of jumping of the ring when the switch is closed in the circuit.
(ii) What will happen if the terminals of the battery are reversed and the switch is closed? Explain.
(iii) Explain the two laws that help us understand this phenomenon.
questions.solution:

questions.stem:
Figure shows the variation of photoelectric current measured in a photocell circuit as a function of the potential difference between the plates of the photo cell when light beams A, B, C and D of different wavelengths are incident on the photo cell. Examine the given figure and answer the following questions:

(i) Which light beam has the highest frequency and why ?
(ii) Which light beam has the longest wavelength and why ?
(iii) Which light beam ejects photoelectrons with maximum momentum and why?
questions.solution:
(i) Graph B shows highest stopping potential which shows that Light beam B has the highest frequency.
(ii) Graph C shows minimum stopping potential which shows that Light beam C has the longest wavelength (or minimum frequency).
(iii) In graph B the light beam eject maximum momentum because frequency is highest so according to Einstein photo electric equation KE will be maximum and momentum also maximum
questions.or_stem: (b) What is the effect on threshold frequency and stopping potential on increasing the frequency of incident beam of light ? Justify your answer.
questions.or_solution:
No change in Threshold frequency because Threshold frequency does not depend on frequency of incident light
Stopping potential increase on increasing the frequency of incident light because as the frequency of incident light increase maximum KE of emitted electron also increase. To stop them completely stopping potential increases
